prompt: A service receives 5 requests a second around the clock. How many requests is that in a day?
hint: Rate times 3,600 times 24.

prompt: The office profile carries fewer requests a month than steady. Why does it still need more capacity at its busiest?
hint: Which of the four numbers decides the size?

choices.text: Its requests run longer than steady's
choices.why: The example gives every profile the same 100 ms.

choices.text: Its idle hours have to be paid in advance
choices.why: Idle hours cost a machine money, but they do not add capacity.

choices.text: Its peak is 60 a second, twice steady's 30
choices.why: Right. Capacity follows the peak, and the volume follows the whole day.

choices.text: Office traffic arrives from more countries
choices.why: Nothing in a profile says where requests come from.

prompt: Requests arrive at random, one a second, and each runs for 100 ms. Roughly how much of the time does an instance have a request inside it?
hint: One minus e to the minus rate times duration.

choices.text: About a tenth
All of it, since there is always a request coming
choices.why: Arriving is not the same as being served; most of each second is empty.

choices.text: Half of it
choices.why: That would need about seven requests a second at 100 ms.

choices.text: None of it, because 100 ms rounds down to zero
choices.why: Nothing rounds the time away; Cloud Run bills in 100 ms steps, not to zero.

prompt: An hour with no request at all is an ___ hour, and it is where the pricing models part company.
hint: It is the third of the four numbers.

prompt: Why does compare.py read its prices from prices.py through a pipe rather than having them typed in?
hint: Where would a second copy of a price go wrong?

choices.text: A pipe is faster than reading constants
choices.why: Speed is not the point; the program runs in a fraction of a second either way.

choices.text: Python cannot hold numbers with eight decimal places
choices.why: It can; prices.py holds them.

choices.text: The pipe fetches today's prices from Google
choices.why: Nothing is fetched; prices.py prints the numbers it holds.

choices.text: Each price lives in one place only
choices.why: Right. No price is typed twice, and a missing one is an error rather than zero.

prompt: For the sparse profile, request-based billing costs 7.37 a month and instance-based 49.93. What explains the gap?
hint: How busy is the instance?

choices.text: Request-based billing has a lower rate per vCPU-second
choices.why: Its rate is higher, 0.000024 against 0.000018.

choices.text: Only the busy tenth of the time is billed
choices.why: Right. Instance-based billing pays for all of the hour.

choices.text: Instance-based billing keeps two instances as a floor
choices.why: The floor of two is for machines and pods; Cloud Run has none in the program.

choices.text: The free tier is applied to request-based billing only
choices.why: The program applies no free tier at all, and says so.

prompt: Instance-based billing costs 0.000019 a second for an instance of 1 vCPU and 512 MiB, and request-based 0.00002525 while serving. Above what busy fraction, in percent and before the fee per request, is instance-based cheaper?
hint: Divide the first by the second.

prompt: At 400 requests a second two e2-standard-2 machines cost 97.84 and Cloud Run billed by request 685.90. Most of that 685.90 is what?
hint: Count the requests in a month.

choices.text: The processor time of four instances
choices.why: That is about 265; the larger part is elsewhere.

choices.text: The load balancer Cloud Run puts in front
choices.why: The program prices no load balancer for any option.

choices.text: The fee of 0.40 per million on about a billion requests a month
choices.why: Right: 420.48 of it.

choices.text: The minimum instances that request-based billing keeps warm
choices.why: The program sets no minimum instances.

prompt: Compute Engine costs 97.84 in every row of the table. Why?
hint: What is the floor, and when is it exceeded?

choices.text: Two machines are the floor, and no profile needs more
choices.why: Right. Even busy fits in two at 200 requests a second each.

choices.text: The program forgot to read the profile for machines
choices.why: It reads it every hour; the result simply never exceeds the floor.

choices.text: Compute Engine prices are fixed monthly, unlike the others
choices.why: They are hourly; 97.84 is two machines for 730 hours.

choices.text: Machines scale to zero in idle hours and back again
choices.why: Nothing stops them in the program; that is why idle hours cost them.

prompt: Which of these does compare.py leave out? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last part of the section lists them.

choices.text: The load balancer machines and pods need
choices.why: Right; Cloud Run has one built in.

choices.text: Cloud Run's monthly free allowances
choices.why: Right; for small profiles they take the bill to nearly nothing.

choices.text: The fee per request under request-based billing
choices.why: It is in: 0.40 per million.

choices.text: Committed use discounts
choices.why: Right; lesson 23 weighs what a commitment ties you to.

choices.text: The GKE cluster management fee
choices.why: It is in the Autopilot column; the free credit is what is left out.

prompt: Which habit of an existing service is called the most expensive to undo before a move?
hint: What does a machine keep by accident?

choices.text: Logging to standard output
choices.why: That is what Cloud Run wants; it costs nothing to keep.

choices.text: Listening on a fixed port such as 8080
choices.why: Reading $PORT is a one-line change.

choices.text: Being written in Python rather than Go
choices.why: Every option here runs either language.

choices.text: State kept on local disk or in memory
choices.why: Right. Every option but a single machine loses it.

prompt: Match each workload to the option its limits leave.
hint: Read the numbers before the prices.

pairs.left: A report that runs for three hours and exits
An HTTP request that takes 40 minutes
A thumbnail made per upload, in seconds
pairs.right: A function triggered by an event

right_distractors: App Engine standard with automatic scaling

prompt: Why does the section rank the options by operations in the opposite order from their price?
hint: Who patches what, after the move?

choices.text: Operations is billed by Google at a higher rate on cheap options
choices.why: Operations is your team's time, not a line on the bill.

choices.text: The cheapest at scale, machines, leave the most work to the team
choices.why: Right. Cloud Run leaves you the container and little else.

choices.text: Managed options need more people to run
choices.why: The reverse: managing is what you pay the provider to do.

choices.text: Machines have no operating system to patch
choices.why: They are the only option where patching is entirely yours.

prompt: A Cloud Run service must finish each request within ___ minutes.
hint: An hour.

prompt: A service stores uploaded files in /tmp and serves them back later. It moves from one machine to Cloud Run with three instances. What happens, and when does anyone notice?
hint: Which instance answers the second request?

choices.text: Cloud Run refuses to deploy a container that writes to /tmp
choices.why: Writing to /tmp is allowed; it is memory, and it is per instance.

choices.text: The files are shared by all three instances automatically
choices.why: Nothing shares an instance's filesystem with another.

choices.text: Downloads fail now and then, once traffic spreads
choices.why: Right. A file lives on the instance that received it, until that instance goes.

choices.text: Uploads become slower but every download still works
choices.why: The cost is correctness, not speed.

prompt: The orders profile sums to 387 requests a second over its 24 hours. How many requests is that in a day?
hint: Each hourly rate lasts 3,600 seconds.

prompt: At ten times today's orders traffic, two e2-standard-2 machines (97.84) beat Cloud Run billed by instance (104.03). Why only then?
hint: Were the machines full before?

choices.text: The machines cost the same, and only now are they full
choices.why: Right. Cloud Run grew with the traffic; the two machines had been idle capacity.

choices.text: Compute Engine gives a volume discount above 400 requests a second
choices.why: No such discount exists in the sheet or the program.

choices.text: Cloud Run raises its price per vCPU-second at high volume
choices.why: The rate is the same; it pays for more instances.

choices.text: Ten times the traffic needs a GPU, which Cloud Run lacks
choices.why: No GPU is involved, and Cloud Run can attach one.

prompt: The nightly export runs for 20 minutes and stops. Where does the worked choice put it?
hint: It is not a service.

choices.text: On a Cloud Run service with a minimum instance
choices.why: A minimum instance pays all day for 20 minutes of work.

choices.text: On an e2-micro left running
choices.why: It would be paid for 24 hours to work for a third of one.

choices.text: On GKE Autopilot, as a Deployment
choices.why: A Deployment keeps pods running; the export should stop.

choices.text: On a Cloud Run job, started by Cloud Scheduler
choices.why: Right. It pays for the 20 minutes and nothing else.

prompt: What is the purpose of the decision table's last column, "revisit when"?
hint: Reasons have an expiry.

choices.text: It schedules the next price review every quarter
choices.why: It names conditions, not dates.

choices.text: It names when the reasons stop being true, not a date
choices.why: Right. It turns a choice into one that can be checked later.

choices.text: It lists the services that will move to GKE next
choices.why: Nothing in the table plans a move to GKE.

choices.text: It records who approved each choice
choices.why: That would be worth keeping, but it is not this column.

prompt: The worked choice runs nothing on Compute Engine or GKE. A colleague concludes the shop should forbid both. What does the section say to that?
hint: A result or a principle?

choices.text: It agrees: serverless is cheaper at every volume
choices.why: The ×10 run shows machines winning; the claim is false.

choices.text: It agrees, since GKE needs a cluster fee
choices.why: A fee is a cost to weigh, not a reason to forbid.

choices.text: It is a result, and a GPU or UDP service would change it
choices.why: Right. The table records reasons, and other reasons give other rows.

choices.text: It disagrees, because GKE is the default for every container
choices.why: There is no such default; the choice is per service.

prompt: Put the steps of choosing compute for a service in the order this lesson follows.
hint: Profile first, decision record last.
items: Rule out options whose limits the workload breaks
Price the remaining options from the sheet
Record the choice with the condition to revisit it
trap: Pricing before ruling out wastes the comparison on options that cannot carry the work.

prompt: Two e2-standard-2 machines cost 97.84 a month. How much is that for a year?
hint: Times twelve.

prompt: A status page gets two requests a second, each of 50 ms, all day. Which Cloud Run billing mode does the arithmetic favour, and why?
hint: Work out the busy fraction: 1 - e^(-2 × 0.05).

choices.text: Request-based: the instance is busy under a tenth of the time
choices.why: Right: about 9.5%, far below the 75% line.

choices.text: Instance-based, because the traffic never stops at any hour
choices.why: Never stopping is not the same as being busy: the instance is empty 90% of the time.

choices.text: Either, because the volume is below the free tier
choices.why: The free tier is left out, and it only applies to request-based billing anyway.

choices.text: Instance-based, because requests of 50 ms are rounded up to a second
choices.why: Cloud Run rounds to 100 ms, not to a second.

prompt: Which profile in the table did Autopilot never win, and why?
hint: Two pods and a fee.

choices.text: Only busy, because pods cannot reach 400 a second
choices.why: Eight pods carried busy; it was the machines that won.

choices.text: Only sparse, because pods cannot scale to zero
choices.why: It lost every row, not one.

choices.text: Only steady, because Autopilot bills per request
choices.why: Autopilot bills for pod resources, per hour.

choices.text: None: two pods plus the fee always lost
choices.why: Right. Autopilot earns its place through operations, which the table does not price.
